text: An access control failure is a function that performs a sensitive action — claiming ownership, withdrawing funds, upgrading logic, destroying a contract — with no check on who is allowed to call it. If a function like that is only ever called once, by the deployer, during setup, a missing access check can sit unnoticed for a long time.

Parity's multisig wallets used a shared library pattern: instead of every wallet deploying its own copy of the logic, each wallet delegatecalled into one shared library contract deployed once. That library had an initWallet function, meant to be called exactly once — and it had no access control on it at all.

In July 2017, a user called initWallet directly on the shared library and became its owner. On November 6th, 2017, that same user called the library's owner-restricted kill function, which ran selfdestruct and wiped the library's code from the blockchain entirely. Every multisig wallet that delegatecalled into that library now pointed at an address with no code at all. Parity's own post-mortem reported the damage: 513,774 ETH frozen across 587 wallets, worth roughly $150 million at the time — no attacker drained a single wallet, but every one of those funds is still sitting there, permanently inaccessible.

The fix is one of Solidity's most well-established patterns: an initialization guard that only allows a setup function to run once, plus an explicit ownership check on anything sensitive after that. 'Only meant to be called once by the deployer' is a comment, not a security control.

This closes the chapter because it's structurally different from the first two lessons — nothing was drained at all. Availability, whether legitimate users can still use their own funds, is a security property just like confidentiality or integrity, and this bug broke it completely without a single successful theft.
